questions.prompt: Why can you install many skills without filling Claude's context window?

options.text: Progressive disclosure: Claude sees only names and descriptions until a skill is relevant
Skills are compressed into a single token
Only one skill can ever be installed
Skills run on a separate server and never use context

questions.explanation: Skills load in layers: front-matter first, the body when relevant, and extra files only when needed.

questions.prompt: A skill's main file, which holds its name, description, and instructions, is called ____.
questions.explanation: Each skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file (the Help Center writes it in lowercase) that starts with YAML front-matter.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a good skill description? Select all that apply.

options.text: Specific trigger situations, like "weekly update" or "status report"

questions.explanation: Claude decides when to load a skill from its description, so state what it does and when to use it. Vague descriptions trigger rarely or randomly.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to add a custom skill to Claude.

items.text: Test prompts that should and shouldn't trigger it
Write the SKILL.md in a folder named after the skill
Upload it in Customize > Skills and turn it on
ZIP the folder so it's at the ZIP's root

questions.explanation: Write the skill, package the folder as the ZIP's root, upload and enable it, then test both triggering and non-triggering prompts.

questions.prompt: Match each feature to what it holds.

pairs.right: A procedure or format loaded when relevant
A bundle of skills, connectors, and sub-agents

questions.explanation: MCP connects Claude to services, skills teach Claude how to do work, projects hold area knowledge, and plugins package them together.

questions.prompt: Why should you only install plugins from trusted sources?

options.text: Plugins can include local MCP servers that run on your computer with your permissions

questions.explanation: The Help Center warns that plugins may include local MCP servers that run on your computer with the same permissions as any other program you run.
